blocks.text: These and other things show more than enough that the אפעה of the Hebrews and the افعى [afʿā] of the Arabs is the viper. Nor is the reason for the name obscure. For in Hebrew פעה means to cry out with a strained voice: hence, therefore, the viper is called אפעה. Avicenna above ^{d)} attributes to it الفحيحة [al-faḥīḥa], that is, a clear hiss. And the Italian mountebanks, on the testimony of Massario in Gesner, call it suffili from its horrible hissing, because, when it is harassed, it gives out such hisses that they are heard a stone's throw away. Further, it is likely that these hisses are strained most of all in giving birth, because it is then afflicted with the sharpest pain. And this is properly פעה. For the verb פעה is not used of just any cry, [col. 364] but of the cry in childbirth. Thus Es. XLII. 14. כיולדה אפעה, like a woman in labour I will cry out ^{(4)}. Hence the Hebrews hold that the Egyptian midwife in Exod. I, 15. was called פועה, because she was customarily called upon with such wailing of women in labour. Accordingly אפעה ephe properly signifies that kind of serpent from which the pains of birth wring a more violent hiss ^{(5)}. This fits the viper above all. Not because its young come out by gnawing through their mother's belly, as the ancients believed. For Theophrastus rightly rejected this as fabulous, and after him Aelian, History book 15, ch. 16. But neither is it certain, as they maintain, that its womb is burst during birth itself because of its narrowness. Certainly the Philosopher does not say that the womb bursts in birth, but the membranes in which the young are wrapped. His words are in the History, book 5, chapter 34: Τίκτει δὲ [III, 133] μικρὰ ἐχίδια ἐν ὑμέσιν, οἳ περιῤῥήγνυνται τριταῖοι [Tiktei de mikra echidia en hymesin, hoi perirrhēgnyntai tritaioi]· It gives birth to small vipers in membranes, which break on the third day. But what follows gave occasion to the fiction: Ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ ἔσωθεν διαφαγόντα αὐτὰ ἐξέρχεται [Eniote de kai esōthen diaphagonta auta exerchetai]· Sometimes also, while they are inside, they gnaw through (not the mother's womb, but the membranes he had mentioned) and come out by themselves. Yet the viper's birth is more difficult for this reason, that it bears live young, whereas the other serpents only hatch eggs. Hence it is called vipera [viper], either as if vi pariat [it gives birth by force], or rather because it is vivipara [viviparous]. From this it is now abundantly clear that אפעה ephe is the viper. And so this rendering fits well enough the three passages of Scripture in which that word occurs, as will be evident to anyone who runs through them.
The first is Iob. XX, 16. תהרגהו לשון אפעה, The tongue of the ephe shall kill him, that is, of the viper, whose bites are deadly even to the hugest beasts. Ovid, book 2 On the Remedy of Love:
The little viper kills the massive bull with its bite.

And in the words The tongue of the ephe shall kill him, what properly belongs to the teeth is attributed to the tongue, because the serpent bites with its tongue thrust out, as if the tongue inflicted the wound. Hence Seneca in Medea 686:
— — — the serpent drags its immense body, and thrusts out its three-forked tongue, and seeks those to whom it may come bringing death. — — — —

And Kimchi on these words of Psalm 140, They have sharpened their tongue like a serpent: חדדו לשונם לדבר רעות כמו הנחש שמחדד לשונו בשבא לנשוך, They have sharpened their tongue to speak evil, as the serpent sharpens its tongue when it prepares to bite.

The second passage is Esa. XXX, 6., where among the Egyptian beasts are reckoned אפעה ושרף מעופף, the ephe and the flying hydrus. For as Egypt nourishes every kind of serpent, so also vipers in great numbers. Ammianus, book 22: Egypt also nourishes countless serpents, raging beyond all deadliness: basilisks, and amphisbaenas, and scytales, and acontiases, and dipsases, and vipers. Indeed the Egyptian vipers have something peculiar. Accordingly Belon describes them specifically in Observations, book 2, ch. 54.

The third passage is Esa. LIX, 5. He who eats of their eggs will die; והזורה תבקע אפעה, and what is crushed, out of it will burst forth an ephe, or viper. What is crushed] In Hebrew הזורה is said here of an egg, as in Iob. XXXIX, 18. of the ostrich's egg: She forgets that a foot תזורה may crush it, and the beast of the field trample it. You will object that eggs cannot be attributed to the viper, because the viper is not ὠοτόκος [ōotokos], oviparous, but ζωοτόκος [zōotokos], viviparous, as we have already noted in passing. And Aristotle expressly [III, 134] asserts it, History book 1, ch. 6: Ἀλλ᾽ οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι ὠοτοκοῦσιν ὄφεις, ἡ δ᾽ ἔχιδνα μόνον ζωοτοκεῖ [All' hoi men alloi ōotokousin opheis, hē d' echidna monon zōotokei]· The other serpents lay eggs, but the viper alone bears a live animal. And Nicander, Theriaca, line 135:
Οἵη γὰρ βαρύθει ὑπὸ κύματι, τοὶ δὲ καθ᾽ ὕλην Ὠοτόκοι ὄφιες λεπυρὴν θάλπουσι γενέθλην. [Hoiē gar barythei hypo kymati, toi de kath' hylēn Ōotokoi ophies lepyrēn thalpousi genethlēn.]
